quote: We study the efficacy of LLMs in generating SCEs via three research questions... We test seven LLMs (7B-70B) across six datasets and four tasks.

We study a specific type of self-explanations: self-generated counterfactual explanations (SCEs). Given an input x and model output ŷ, a counterfactual x CE is a modified input that leads the model to output ŷCE ̸ = ŷ.

We use the following metrics for evaluating SCEs... Counterfactual validity (Val) measures the percentage of times the SCE actually produces the intended target label... Edit distance (ED) measures the edit distance between the original input x and the counterfactual x CE.

We use the following metrics for evaluating SCEs. Generation percentage (Gen) measures the percentage of times a model was able to generate a SCE. ... Counterfactual validity (Val) measures the percentage of times the SCE actually produces the intended target label, i.e., f (x CE ) = y CE . ... Edit distance (ED) measures the edit distance between the original input x and the counterfactual x CE .
Finally, we ask the model to make a prediction on its generated counterfactual, namely, ŷ CE = f (x CE )... We denote the validity without context as Val and with context as Val C.

Our goal was to test if the SCE validity correlates with its correctness. To this end, for each model, we annotated SCE correctness (that is, if the SCE indeed evaluates to the target label) on 50 randomly selected GSM8K samples. The annotation protocol is reported in Appendix G.
guideline: Annotators assessed whether SCEs produced solutions matching target labels; disagreements resolved through discussion
Annotators were asked to judge whether each self‑generated counterfactual explanation produced the correct target answer.

The annotation protocol is reported in Appendix G. Each example was independently assessed by two annotators (the authors), who determined whether the SCE yielded a solution matching the correct target label (ŷ CE ).
